title: 12 Best TypeScript AI Agent Frameworks in 2026

blocks.text: 12 Best TypeScript AI Agent Frameworks in 2026

Best TypeScript AI agent frameworks in 2026: Vercel AI SDK, Mastra, LangChain.js, Cloudflare Agents SDK and the official OpenAI, Claude and Google agent SDKs, 12 ranked with real tradeoffs and a use-case guide.

The best TypeScript AI agent frameworks in 2026: the Vercel AI SDK for streaming chat and tool-calling UIs on Next.js, Mastra for full-stack agent apps with workflows and memory, and LangChain.js for integration breadth and explicit graph control flow via LangGraph.js. If your agent lives or dies on structured output, Ax and BAML are the strongest picks. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google now all ship official TypeScript agent SDKs too, and we cover each one. Stop reading here and you already have the answer for most projects: AI SDK for chat products, Mastra for agent products. If you need a production Next.js AI app built with RAG, agents, and evals already wired up, our Next.js AI app development service handles model integration through Vercel deploy.

TypeScript stopped being the runner-up language for AI agents in 2025. Full-stack type safety from the model call to the React component pulled most new product teams onto the TS side, and the hard part now is separating frameworks that are production-ready from the long tail of half-built abstractions on GitHub. Many ship a flashy README and a demo video, then go quiet by the next release. We focused on frameworks that either have a serious vendor behind them, a real maintainer in mid-2026, or a published track record of running in user-facing products.

This guide compares the 12 best TypeScript AI agent frameworks in 2026 with real capabilities, honest pricing, pros and cons, and a framework to pick the right one. We ranked on production readiness first, then TypeScript ergonomics, then maintenance activity. For the four entries added in September 2026 (OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, Google ADK for TypeScript, and Genkit), every license and release number comes from the official repo or npm listing, checked on 2026-09-26. No hands-on testing is claimed for those four.

Last checked: October 2026 (licenses, versions and pricing re-verified on 2026-10-21). Two entries were dropped because their maintainers archived them: LlamaIndex.TS (deprecated by LlamaIndex) and Agentic (archived by its author in February 2026). Cloudflare Agents SDK and Strands Agents for TypeScript take their places at the end of the list. Pair it with our AI agent development service and the best Claude Code GitHub repos for context on the broader ecosystem.
Best TypeScript AI agent frameworks: a brief overview
Vercel AI SDK: Best for streaming chat and tool-calling UIs on Next.js: the most-installed TS agent toolkit, model-agnostic and production-hardened.
Mastra: Best for full-stack agent apps with workflows, memory, and evals: opinionated TS framework from the Gatsby team.

LangChain.js: Best for porting Python LangChain patterns to TS: largest TS agent ecosystem, deep integration coverage. (If your team prefers Python outright, see our best Python AI agent frameworks guide.)
OpenAI Agents SDK (JS/TS): Best for handoffs, guardrails, and voice agents: OpenAI's official MIT-licensed agent SDK with realtime support.
Claude Agent SDK (TypeScript): Best for agents that edit files and run commands: the Claude Code agent loop as a library.
Google ADK for TypeScript: Best for multi-agent workflows on Gemini and Google Cloud: code-first, Apache 2.0, runs in Node.js and the browser.
Genkit: Best for full-stack AI features on Firebase and Google Cloud: production-ready JS/TS SDK with a local Developer UI.
VoltAgent: Best for observability-first agent development: open-source TS framework with a built-in visual debugger.
Ax (AxLLM): Best for DSPy-style typed signatures in TypeScript: brings programmatic prompts and self-optimization to TS.
BAML: Best for structured output and schema-first prompts: a typed language for agent functions you call from TypeScript.
Cloudflare Agents SDK: Best for stateful, per-user agents on Cloudflare Workers: MIT-licensed, built on Durable Objects.
Strands Agents (TypeScript): Best for AWS and Amazon Bedrock teams: Apache 2.0 agent SDK announced by AWS, with Graph and Swarm multi-agent patterns.
1. Vercel AI SDK, best for streaming chat and tool-calling UIs on Next.js

The Vercel AI SDK is the default starting point for most TypeScript agent projects in 2026. It is model-agnostic, ships first-class React and Next.js hooks, and has become the reference implementation for streaming UI, tool calling, and structured generation in TS. Most production chat products you have used recently are built on it, whether they advertise it or not. Vercel maintains the SDK directly and ships breaking changes on a predictable cadence.

The SDK pairs cleanly with Server Components, the App Router, and edge runtimes. For teams that already deploy on Vercel, it removes most of the glue code between a model provider and a chat interface, and it now covers full agent loops with generateText, streamText, and tool definitions in one typed surface.
Key features
Unified API across OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI, Mistral, Bedrock, and more
First-class streaming with useChat, useCompletion, and RSC support
Typed tool calling with Zod schemas, plus ToolLoopAgent and the durable WorkflowAgent (from @ai-sdk/workflow) for agent loops
Structured output via generateText and streamText with an output setting (generateObject and streamObject are deprecated)
AI Gateway integration for routing, observability, and provider failover
Best for
Next.js teams building chat or agent UIs
Product engineers who want streaming-by-default
Teams already invested in the Vercel platform
Pricing
Free and open-source under Apache 2.0
Optional AI Gateway charges provider list prices with no markup and includes free monthly credits on a subset of models
Pros
Largest community and most up-to-date provider coverage in TS
Excellent docs, plus a migration guide and codemods for each major version (v7 is current as of October 2026)
Deep integration with the Next.js rendering model
Backed by a vendor with a clear commercial incentive to keep it healthy
Cons
Less opinionated about agent architecture than Mastra or LangChain.js
Heavier React bias; non-React frontends use a smaller slice of the surface
AI SDK 7 requires Node.js 22 or later and is ESM-only, so CommonJS projects need a migration first
Free weekly brief
Steal our production automations
The exact n8n flows, Claude Code setups, and prompts we ship for clients, broken down step by step. No spam, unsubscribe anytime.
2. Mastra, best for full-stack agent apps with workflows, memory, and evals

Mastra is the most ambitious "batteries-included" TypeScript agent framework to emerge in 2025. Built by the team behind Gatsby and now an independent company, it bundles agents, workflows, memory, RAG, evals, and a local dev UI into a single TS-first framework. Where the Vercel AI SDK gives you primitives, Mastra gives you opinions, and the opinions are usually right for teams shipping a real product.

It runs anywhere Node runs, including Vercel, Cloudflare Workers, and your own infra, and ships a local playground that lets you inspect agent traces, tool calls, and memory state without wiring up extra observability. For Claude Code-style agent products built in TypeScript, Mastra has become the default scaffold.
Key features
Agents with typed tools, memory, and structured output
Step-based workflows with branching, suspend/resume, and human-in-the-loop
Built-in vector stores and RAG primitives
Evals framework for regression-testing agent behavior
Local dev UI with traces, memory inspection, and replay
Best for
Teams building agent-native products that go beyond chat
TS-first engineering orgs that want one framework end to end
Anyone who wants workflows and evals without gluing five tools together
Pricing
Free and open-source under Apache 2.0 (code in ee/ directories uses a separate enterprise license)
Hosted Mastra Platform: free Starter plan, Teams at $250/month (mastra.ai/pricing, October 2026)
Pros
Most cohesive TS agent framework on the market in 2026
Strong default architecture for non-trivial agents
Active maintenance, weekly releases, responsive maintainers
Plays well with the Vercel AI SDK underneath
Cons
Younger than LangChain.js, smaller integration catalog
Opinionated structure can feel heavy for tiny side projects
3. LangChain.js, best for porting Python LangChain patterns to TS

LangChain.js is the TypeScript sibling of the most-used agent framework in Python. It is no longer a 1:1 port; the JS version has its own release cadence, its own LangGraph.js companion library, and a growing set of integrations. For teams that already use LangChain on the Python side, or that need an integration that does not exist anywhere else in TS, LangChain.js is still the path of least resistance.

LangGraph.js, the stateful graph runtime, has become the most interesting part of the stack. It models agents as graphs with explicit nodes, edges, and state, which makes complex multi-step agents far easier to debug than free-form prompt chains.
Key features
LangGraph.js for stateful, typed agent graphs
Largest integration catalog in TS: vector DBs, tools, loaders, retrievers
LangSmith integration for tracing, evals, and prompt management
Prebuilt agent patterns: ReAct, plan-and-execute, multi-agent
First-party support for streaming and tool calling
Best for
Teams already standardized on LangChain in Python
Complex multi-step agents that benefit from explicit graph state
Use cases requiring a niche integration not yet in Mastra or the AI SDK
Pricing
Free and open-source under MIT
LangSmith (observability/evals) is free up to a usage cap, then paid
Pros
Mature, with the deepest integration coverage in TypeScript
LangGraph.js is genuinely good for non-trivial agent control flow
Tightly coupled with LangSmith for production observability
Familiar to anyone coming from Python LangChain
Cons
API surface is large and historically churny
Some abstractions add indirection you may not need
4. OpenAI Agents SDK (JS/TS), best for handoffs, guardrails, and voice agents

The OpenAI Agents SDK for JavaScript and TypeScript is OpenAI's official agent framework, published on npm as @openai/agents under the MIT license. Its README calls it provider-agnostic, supporting OpenAI APIs and more. The core idea is small: agents with instructions and tools, handoffs between agents, guardrails on input and output, and tracing for every run.

What sets it apart in TypeScript is the Realtime side. The same package ships RealtimeAgent and RealtimeSession for low-latency voice agents in the browser, plus sandbox agents that work inside a filesystem workspace and run commands for longer tasks. If your roadmap includes a voice agent, one package covers both the text and the voice side.
Key features
Agents with instructions, tools, guardrails, and handoffs
Agents as tools, so one agent can call another for a subtask
Realtime agents for spoken, low-latency interactions in the browser
Sandbox agents with a filesystem workspace for longer-running work
Built-in tracing, sessions for conversation history, and human-in-the-loop approvals
Best for
Teams building on OpenAI models who want the vendor's own agent patterns
Voice and realtime agent products
Multi-agent triage flows where one agent routes to specialists
Pricing
Free and open-source under MIT
You pay for model usage with whichever provider you call
Latest release when we checked on 2026-10-21: v0.21.0 (October 20, 2026)
Pros
Maintained by OpenAI, with docs and examples for every core concept
Realtime voice agents in the same package as text agents
Small API: an agent, a run() call, and handoffs cover most use cases
Cons
Still pre-1.0 (v0.21.0 when checked), so expect API changes between minor versions
Requires Node.js 22 or later, and Cloudflare Workers support is marked experimental
Skip it if you deploy to an older Node runtime or want a framework with built-in workflows, memory stores, and evals in one package. Mastra covers that better.
5. Claude Agent SDK (TypeScript), best for agents that work on files and run commands

The Claude Agent SDK is Anthropic's library for running the Claude Code agent loop inside your own application. The TypeScript package is @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk. Anthropic's docs describe it as the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code, programmable in Python and TypeScript. If you want the difference in detail, read our Claude Agent SDK vs Claude Code breakdown.

This is not a general-purpose model wrapper. It is the right pick when the agent's job is to read a codebase, edit files, run shell commands, and finish multi-step tasks with permissions and approvals, which is what Claude Code already does well.
Key features
Built-in tools to read, write, and edit files, run commands, and search the web
Hooks that run your code at key points in the agent lifecycle
Subagents for focused subtasks
MCP support for external tools and data sources
Permissions, plus sessions you can resume or fork later
Best for
Coding agents, internal dev tools, and repo automation
Teams that already use Claude Code and want the same behavior inside a product
Agents that need approval gates before running tools
Pricing
The SDK is free to install; use is governed by Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service, not an open-source license
You pay for Claude API usage with an API key
Latest release when we checked on 2026-10-21: v0.3.306 (October 21, 2026)
Pros
Gives you a production agent loop, file tools, and permissions without building them
Loads skills, commands, and memory from .claude/ the same way Claude Code does
Very frequent releases from Anthropic
Cons
Built around Claude models, so it is the wrong base for a multi-provider product
Not open-source licensed, which matters if your legal team requires OSS dependencies
Skip it if you need a chat UI toolkit or want to swap model providers freely. The Vercel AI SDK fits that job better.
6. Google ADK for TypeScript, best for multi-agent workflows on Gemini and Google Cloud

Agent Development Kit (ADK) for TypeScript is Google's code-first agent framework, published as @google/adk under Apache 2.0. The README says it runs in Node.js and the browser, with full type safety, Zod schema validation, and ESM, CommonJS, and web bundles. It is the TypeScript sibling of the Python ADK we cover in best multi-agent frameworks.

ADK's strength is orchestration. You compose agents into sequential, parallel, loop, and routed workflows, and delegate to remote agents over the A2A protocol. A separate dev tools package gives you a CLI and a web UI for testing agents locally.
Key features
Tool parameters typed with Zod v3 or v4, with compile-time inference
Sequential, parallel, loop, and routed multi-agent workflows
Built-in tools for Google Search, Google Maps, Vertex AI Search, and URL context
MCP server connections and remote agents over A2A
@google/adk-devtools CLI and dev UI, plus a deploy command for Cloud Run
Best for
Teams on Google Cloud or Gemini
Multi-agent systems that need explicit workflow shapes
Orgs running ADK in Python who want the same model in TypeScript
Pricing
Free and open-source under Apache 2.0
Gemini, Vertex AI, and Cloud Run usage is billed separately if you use them
Latest release when we checked on 2026-10-21: v2.3.0 (October 13, 2026)
Pros
Maintained by Google, with shared concepts across the Python and TypeScript versions
Runs in the browser as well as on the server
Workflow agents make multi-agent control flow explicit instead of prompt-driven
Cons
The quick start and built-in tools lean on Gemini and Google services
Needs Node.js 20.19 or newer, and v2.0.0 only shipped in August 2026, so community examples are still thin
Skip it if your stack is AWS or Azure and you have no plan to use Gemini. You will spend time working around Google defaults.
7. Genkit, best for full-stack AI features on Firebase and Google Cloud

Genkit is an open-source framework from Google's Firebase team for building AI-powered applications. Its README lists the JavaScript/TypeScript SDK as production-ready with full feature support, alongside Go, Python (beta), and Dart (preview). The genkit npm package is Apache 2.0.

Genkit sits between the AI SDK and a full agent framework. You get a unified model interface through plugins for Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, and others, plus flows, tool calling, structured output, RAG, and a local Developer UI that shows traces for every run.
Key features
Unified model API through provider plugins
Flows for multi-step AI workflows, with tool calling and structured output
Dotprompt templates for managing prompts as files
